LTF-A0-to-B1-Course-Outline.content:
A0 to B1 Course Outline
The French Reading Textbook is the language precision layer of Proustian.
French is not an independent general course here. The goal is accelerated reading toward Proust by ignoring irrelevant general French topics while preserving essential reading grammar.
Plan first: A0 to B1, roughly 50-60 chapters.
Pace: about one chapter per week.
Sequence Rationale
The opening sequence follows reading-knowledge French textbook tradition:

cognates and visual recognition
false friends and controlled guessing
word families and recognition patterns
function words and relation marking
sentence structure

This sequence trains reading actions before interpretation. It also supports U1’s method: recognition first, claim second, textual return always.
Stage 0 — A0 — Seeing French
Goal: see the French sentence before interpretation.
Core work:

sentence boundaries
subject and verb
nouns, gender, and number
articles
basic word order
English structural control

Prototype chapters:

Recognizing French on the Page: Cognates and Reading Confidence
When English Misleads: False Friends and Controlled Guessing
Word Families: Suffixes, Prefixes, and Recognition Patterns
Function Words I: Small Words That Control Reading
What Is a French Sentence?

Stage 1 — A1 — Reading Skeleton
Goal: read simple French sentence skeletons.
Core work:

être and avoir
regular present tense
adjectives and agreement
prepositions
negation
basic objects and complements

Stage 2 — A2 — Narrative Memory Grammar
Goal: read basic narrative and memory structures.
Core work:

passé composé
imparfait
past-tense contrast
participles
infinitives
modal verbs
time expressions

Stage 3 — B1 — Proustian Entry
Goal: enter controlled Proustian reading.
Core work:

relative clauses
que-clauses
subordinate material
delayed main verbs
apposition
parenthesis
accumulated modifiers
short Proust-oriented micro-readings

LTF-Chapter-001-Cognates-and-Reading-Con.content:
Chapter 001 — Recognizing French on the Page
Subtitle: Cognates and Reading Confidence
What You Will Learn
You will learn that you are not starting from nothing. Many French literary and intellectual words resemble English words closely enough to give you an initial foothold.
You will also learn the first rule of this course: recognition is useful, but recognition is not mastery.
Why This Matters
A French page can look opaque before you know how to look at it. But an English reader can often recognize words such as mémoire, sensation, impression, attention, and perception.
These words do not make the sentence easy. They make the sentence approachable.
1. Cognates
A cognate is a word that resembles a word in another language because of shared history or borrowing.
Examples:





























FrenchEnglish supportmémoirememorysensationsensationimpressionimpressionattentionattentionperceptionperception
The English support word is not a final translation. It is a first handle.
2. Recognition Is Not Mastery
When you see a recognizable French word, do not stop reading.
Use this rule:

Notice the familiar shape.
Give yourself a simple English support word.
Mark uncertainty.
Continue through the sentence.

For example:
mémoire may point toward memory, but the sentence will decide whether it means memory as faculty, recollection, record, or something more specific.
3. Reading Before Interpreting
The first reading action is controlled recognition.
You are not trying to produce a polished translation. You are learning to keep moving through the French line without panic.
Ask:

What word looks familiar?
What English support word helps me continue?
What must remain uncertain until I see the sentence?

Core Vocabulary






































































FrenchEnglish supportCautionmémoirememoryMay mean faculty, recollection, or record.sensationsensationContext decides force.impressionimpressionMay be mental, sensory, or artistic.attentionattentionOften tied to perception and judgment.perceptionperceptionUseful abstract noun.imageimageMay be visual, mental, or literary.formeformMay mean shape or artistic form.possiblepossibleHigh-confidence cognate.visiblevisibleHigh-confidence cognate.naturenatureMeaning depends on context.silencesilenceHigh-confidence cognate.momentmomentHigh-confidence cognate.
Reading Examples

Une sensation.
Une impression visible.
La mémoire.
Une image possible.
Le silence.
Un moment.
La forme visible.
Une perception.

Practice
Give an English support word. Do not try to translate a full sentence yet.

mémoire
sensation
impression
attention
perception
image
forme
visible
silence
moment

Review Check

What is a cognate?
Why is recognition useful?
Why is recognition not mastery?
What should you do after recognizing a familiar-looking word?
Why should uncertainty remain open until the sentence is read?

What to Remember
French is not completely opaque to an English reader.
Recognizable words give you a foothold.
A foothold is not a full interpretation. Keep reading.

LTF-Chapter-002-False-Friends-and-Contro.content:
Chapter 002 — When English Misleads
Subtitle: False Friends and Controlled Guessing
What You Will Learn
In this chapter you will learn what false friends are, why English resemblance can both help and mislead, how to guess safely, and how to correct a wrong first impression.
You are not being told to distrust every familiar-looking French word. You are learning to use resemblance carefully. English can give you a clue, but the French sentence must decide.
Why This Matters
French and English share many words. This is useful for reading. It means that a beginner can often recognize part of a French page before knowing much grammar.
But resemblance is not proof. A French word may look like English and still mean something different. A reader must learn to use English as a clue, not as a master.
This matters for Proust because first impressions are powerful. They are also often incomplete. Reading well means noticing the first impression, then checking it against the sentence.
1. The Problem: Familiar Words Can Betray You
Some French words look friendly because they resemble English. The danger is that the familiar shape makes you too confident.
Examples:

actuellement does not mean “actually.” It means currently or at present.
attendre does not mean “attend.” It means to wait for.
librairie does not mean “library.” It means bookstore.

The mistake is understandable. The words look familiar. But reading French requires a second step: check whether the familiar-looking English word actually fits the French sentence.
2. Three Kinds of Traps
2.1 False Friends
A false friend is a word that looks like an English word but means something different.
Example:
déception looks like “deception,” but it usually means disappointment.
2.2 Partial Cognates
A partial cognate has an English-like meaning in some contexts but not all.
Example:
expérience can mean experience, but it can also mean experiment. The sentence decides.
2.3 Expression Traps
Sometimes the individual word looks familiar, but the phrase works differently.
Example:
assister à means to attend or be present at.
Do not read assister à as “to assist.” The small word à is part of the expression.
3. Controlled Guessing
Controlled guessing is a safe way to use resemblance.

Notice resemblance.
Make a tentative guess.
Check the word type.
Check the sentence.
Replace the guess if it fails.
Read again.

Example:
Le lecteur attend.
Bad first guess:
“The reader attends.”
Better reading:
“The reader waits.”
Why? attend is a French verb form from attendre, meaning to wait for.
4. Core False Friends

Read these slowly. Do not rush from resemblance to interpretation.

Il assiste à une scène.

Une erreur grave change la lecture.
Cette histoire reste difficile.

6. Practice: Correct the Guess
For each item, replace the bad guess with a safer reading.


French word: actuellement
Bad guess: actually
Correct reading:

Bad guess: attend

7. Practice: Read the Sentence
Choose the safer English reading.


Le lecteur attend.
A. The reader attends.
B. The reader waits.


La lecture devient difficile.
A. The lecture becomes difficult.
B. The reading becomes difficult.


Une déception transforme le souvenir.
A. A disappointment transforms the memory.
B. A deception transforms the memory.


Le narrateur ignore la cause.
A. The narrator ignores the cause.
B. The narrator does not know the cause.


Une impression sensible apparaît.
A. A perceptible impression appears.
B. A sensible impression appears.


Il assiste à une scène.
A. He assists a scene.
B. He attends / is present at a scene.


La mémoire reste obscure.
A. Memory remains obscure.
B. Memory rests obscure.


Dans le coin, une image revient.
A. In the corner, an image returns.
B. In the coin, an image returns.


Sa propre mémoire revient.
A. His own memory returns.
B. His proper memory returns.


Cette histoire reste difficile.
A. This story / history remains difficult.
B. This history must always mean academic history.


8. Review Check

What is a false friend?
Why is actuellement dangerous for an English reader?
What does attendre mean?
What is the difference between a false friend and a partial cognate?
Why should you check word type before paraphrasing?
What does assister à mean?
Why is déception not usually “deception”?
What should you do when the English-looking guess makes a strange sentence?
How does controlled guessing protect reading?
Why is resemblance a clue but not proof?

9. What to Remember
English resemblance is a clue.
A clue is not proof.
Guess, verify, and reread.
False friends are not just exceptions to memorize. They are training devices for judgment. They teach you to pause before interpretation and to return to the French sentence.

LTF-Chapter-003-Word-Families-and-Recogn.content:
Chapter 003 — Word Families
Subtitle: Suffixes, Prefixes, and Recognition Patterns
What You Will Learn
You will learn to recognize groups of related words instead of memorizing isolated vocabulary one item at a time.
Why This Matters
Reading grows faster when you can see patterns. A suffix, prefix, or spelling clue can help you connect a new French word to an English support word.
1. Suffix Patterns
Some French endings are strongly recognizable to English readers.



































French patternExampleEnglish support-tionattentionattention-itésensibilitésensibility-mentmouvementmovement-able / -iblevisiblevisible-if / -iveactif / activeactive
2. Prefix and Spelling Clues
Some words preserve older spelling relationships.
Examples:

étude can be linked to study.
forêt can be linked to forest.

The circumflex often marks a historical spelling change. It is not a rule you can use blindly, but it can help recognition.
3. Pattern Recognition
When you see a new word, ask:

Does it have a familiar ending?
Does it belong to a known word family?
Does the English support word fit the sentence?

Core Vocabulary

































































FrenchPatternEnglish supportattention-tionattentionperception-tionperceptionsensation-tionsensationsensibilité-itésensibilitymouvement-mentmovementvisible-iblevisiblepossible-iblepossibleactif-ifactiveactive-iveactiveétudespelling relationstudyforêtcircumflex clueforest
Reading Examples

Une attention visible.
La perception change.
Une sensation revient.
La sensibilité apparaît.
Le mouvement devient possible.
Une image active.

Practice
Name the pattern.

attention
perception
sensibilité
mouvement
visible
actif
active
forêt

Review Check

Why are word families useful?
What English pattern often matches French -tion?
What does -ment often suggest?
Why should pattern recognition still be checked in the sentence?

What to Remember
Vocabulary is not only a list. It is a network of forms.
Patterns help you recognize more, but the sentence still decides meaning.

LTF-Chapter-004-Function-Words-I.content:
Chapter 004 — Function Words I
Subtitle: Small Words That Control Reading
What You Will Learn
You will learn that small French words often control how a sentence is built.
Why This Matters
Readers often notice nouns and verbs first. But long French sentences are held together by relation words. If you skip small words, you lose the structure.
1. Relation Words
Function words show relation, direction, contrast, location, addition, or comparison.













































FrenchBasic reading valuedeof / from / relationàto / at / towardetandmaisbutdansin / insidesuron / uponavecwithsanswithoutcommeas / like
2. Do Not Translate Too Quickly
A function word may have more than one English value.
For example, de can suggest of, from, relation, source, or possession. You should not choose too quickly. First ask what it connects.
3. Attachment
The main question is:
What does this small word attach?
Example:
dans la mémoire
dans places something inside a frame: in memory.
Core Vocabulary













































FrenchReading actiondemark relationàmark direction or targetetaddmaiscontrastdansplace inside a framesurplace on / uponavecjoin withsansmark absencecommecompare
Reading Examples

dans la mémoire
avec une sensation
sans image
le temps et la mémoire
une impression de silence
comme une image
sur la table
à la chambre

Practice
Name the relation.

dans la mémoire
avec une sensation
sans image
le temps et la mémoire
mais la mémoire revient
comme une impression

Review Check

Why should small words not be skipped?
What does mais usually do?
What does sans mark?
What question should you ask when you see de?

What to Remember
Small words are not decorative.
They tell you how parts of the sentence attach.

LTF-Chapter-005-What-Is-a-French-Sentenc.content:
Chapter 005 — What Is a French Sentence?
Subtitle: Subject, Verb, Complement, Modifier
What You Will Learn
You will learn to see the basic parts of a French sentence before trying to interpret it.
Why This Matters
Even a long Proustian sentence is built from grammatical relations. Before you interpret, you must find the structure.
1. Subject and Verb
The subject is what the sentence is about.
The conjugated verb is the action, state, or movement of the sentence.
Example:
Le souvenir revient.
Subject: Le souvenir
Verb: revient
2. Complements
A complement completes the meaning of a verb or phrase.
Example:
Le temps transforme l'impression.
Subject: Le temps
Verb: transforme
Complement: l'impression
3. Modifiers
A modifier adds description, place, time, or condition.
Example:
Dans la mémoire, une image revient.
Modifier: Dans la mémoire
Subject: une image
Verb: revient
Core Vocabulary

















































FrenchEnglish supportle souvenirmemory / recollectionla chambreroomle tempstimela mémoirememoryune sensationa sensationune impressionan impressionrevenirto returnsemblerto seemapparaîtreto appeartransformerto transform
Reading Examples

Le souvenir revient.
La chambre semble silencieuse.
Une sensation apparaît.
Le temps transforme l'impression.
Dans la mémoire, une image revient.

Practice
For each sentence, find the subject and verb.

Le souvenir revient.
Une sensation apparaît.
La chambre semble silencieuse.
Le temps transforme l'impression.
Dans la mémoire, une image revient.

Review Check

What is a subject?
What is a conjugated verb?
What is a complement?
What is a modifier?
Why should structure come before interpretation?

What to Remember
Do not translate before you see the sentence.
Find the subject. Find the verb. Then ask what completes or modifies the sentence.
Next Chapter
Chapter 006 is paused until Chapters 001–005 have been deepened and used.

LTF-Course-Architecture.title: LTF-Course-Architecture
LTF-Course-Architecture.content:
French Reading Textbook
The French Reading Textbook is the language precision layer of Proustian.
It is not a generic French course. It is a reading course built toward Proust.
French is the target language. English is the scaffold language. Chinese is not the main scaffold for this track.
The first planning horizon is A0 to B1, roughly 50-60 chapters, at about one chapter per week.
Pedagogical Reliability
This is a targeted reading curriculum, not AI-generated improvisation.
It combines:

reading-knowledge French textbook tradition
classical-language reading textbook rigor
evidence-informed instructed SLA principles
input processing and form-meaning mapping
Anki repetition
self-tested diagnostic revision
Proust-specific target pressure

Ordinary French textbooks serve general language ability. This textbook serves reading competence toward Proust. It may skip conversation, travel situations, and general communicative tasks, but it must not skip reading grammar, vocabulary recognition, function words, reference, tense, subordination, or long-sentence parsing.

English Scaffold Policy
French is the target language and final textual object.
English is the scaffold language:

explanations
grammar labels
literal control readings
natural paraphrases
comparison notes
structural checks
answer-key explanations

Chinese is not the main scaffold for the French Reading Textbook. It may appear only in meta/project notes if necessary.
Required learner-facing labels:

Literal English Control
Natural English Paraphrase
Structural Check
English Reading Note

Avoid:

Chinese paraphrase drills
Chinese-French translation exercises inside French textbook chapters
translation-training workflows inside French textbook chapters
literary essay commentary inside A0 grammar lessons

LTF-Proust-Target-Policy.title: LTF-Proust-Target-Policy
LTF-Proust-Target-Policy.content:
Proust Target Policy
The final target is Marcel Proust, À la recherche du temps perdu, in French.
The first book is not yet direct Proust reading. Early chapters prepare the reader for Proust by building structural sight.
Use Proust-oriented vocabulary when it helps:

memory
time
rooms
sensation
perception
signs
sentence movement
narration

Do not force fake Proustian depth into A0 lessons.
Model sentences may be controlled or adapted. They must be clearly marked as training sentences when they are not quotations.
Long Proust quotations should wait until the reader has enough grammar to parse them.

Vocabulary Progression
Vocabulary should support reading grammar and Proustian preparation.
Progression:

Cognates
False friends
Word families
Function words
Proust lexical fields
Proust-oriented micro-readings

Principles

Use high-yield reading vocabulary before topic vocabulary.
Teach function words early and repeatedly.
Mark false friends clearly.
Use Proust-oriented vocabulary without forcing fake Proustian depth into A0 lessons.
Keep vocabulary tied to sentence reading, not isolated memorization.
Treat vocabulary as a repeatable recognition system, not a list.
Convert vocabulary into cards only when each card tests one retrievable point.
Use failed cards to revise vocabulary presentation.

Acquisition Loop
cognate recognition → false friend warning → word family → function word → Proust lexical field → sentence encounter → Anki card → failed-card diagnosis → re-encounter

Purpose
This page gathers the first usable reading entrances for Proustian 2.0. It does not replace reading. It gives the reader a small number of passages, questions, and directions from which reading can begin.

Locate the passage.
read the passage.
write one question.
turn the question into a Passage Card.

Question-Gradient.title: Question-Gradient
Question-Gradient.content:
Question Gradient
Root Question
How does Proust train the reader to discover truth through signs, sensation, attention, misrecognition, and artistic form?
Starting Questions

What sign appears before it is understood?
What kind of sensation starts the reading process?
What kind of delay, mistake, or misrecognition organizes the scene?
What secondary lens clarifies the passage without replacing Proust?
What form of attention does the passage train?
How can this passage become a reader-facing card?

U1｜Signs / Method
How does Proust train the reader to read signs rather than merely follow plot, psychology, or memory?
Method entrance:

U1 General Introduction: From the Memory Cliché to Polycentric Reading

Supporting questions:

What forces thought before interpretation begins?
What makes a sign readable?
How does Deleuze help without replacing Proust?

U2｜Memory / Time / Space
How does Proust transform memory from recollection into a structure of signs, time, space, and artistic discovery?
Supporting questions:

How does the Madeleine scene turn sensation into discovery?
How does involuntary memory reopen time through place and sensation?
How does habit shape what can or cannot be perceived?

U3｜Music / Ineffable
How does Vinteuil’s music move from emotional sign to artistic truth, ineffable experience, and novelistic structure?
Supporting questions:

How does music carry truth before it can be explained?
How does the little phrase move from love sign to art sign?
What does the ineffable allow the novel to think?

U4｜Visuality / Gaze / Photography / Attention
How does Proust transform seeing into a discipline of attention, misrecognition, capture, and artistic truth?
Supporting questions:

How does the Vermeer yellow wall become a test of attention?
How does seeing differ from understanding?
How do gaze, framing, and capture organize misrecognition?

U5｜Space / Sensory History
How do spaces and sensory environments in Proust produce social time and historical subjectivity?
Supporting questions:

How do rooms and salons become social machines?
How do bells gather collective time?
How do smell and atmosphere mark social boundaries?

U6｜Writing Apparatus
How can U1–U5 be transformed into teachable, writable, reader-facing forms without losing aesthetic and intellectual force?
Supporting questions:

How does a Passage Card become a reader-facing block?
How does a Unit Digest become a course page?
How does the website remain a reading garden rather than a content dump?

Active Questions

Which golden entrance should become the first real Passage Card?
What passage boundary can be verified tonight?
What question does the passage answer?

Paused Questions

Full bibliography expansion
Full Zotero workflow
Full folder restructuring
Full music history expansion
Full art history expansion
Full Annales / sociology expansion

U1-General-Introduction-Memory-Cliche-to.title: U1｜General Introduction: From the Memory Cliché to Polycentric Reading
U1-General-Introduction-Memory-Cliche-to.content:
U1｜General Introduction: From the Memory Cliché to Polycentric Reading
U1 is not a signs unit. It is the general introduction that uses the memory cliché as a methodological hinge: from involuntary memory to competing reading lenses, from single-center interpretation to claim/problem chains, and finally back to Proust’s textual world.
Position｜U1 as General Introduction
U1 establishes the course’s methodological tendency. It does not ask the reader to replace memory with signs, nor to choose Deleuze as the master key. It shows how the cliché “Proust is a novelist of memory” becomes the first pressure point from which the whole course opens.
Not This｜Signs as Course Center
U1 should not make “signs” into a new sovereign center. Deleuze remains useful, but he is only one theoretical line among several.
But This｜Memory Cliché as Methodological Hinge
The course begins with the force and insufficiency of involuntary memory, then unfolds multiple reading paths that return to the novel.

Core formulation: U1 is a methodological overture. It explains how Proustian 2.0 reads through strong theoretical positions without allowing any one of them to own Proust.

The Memory Cliché as Starting Pressure
The tradition of involuntary memory is not a weak opponent. It is powerful enough to become a recurring object of criticism, compression, displacement, and renewal. U1 must therefore begin by granting its force before showing why it cannot remain the only center.
English Claim
Memory is powerful but insufficient.
Proust is often entered through lost time, involuntary memory, and the return of the personal past. This entry is legitimate, but incomplete. If memory becomes the first and final explanation, the novel’s errors, delays, social codes, musical pressures, visual fragments, and artistic discoveries are flattened.
中文判断
记忆是强传统，但不是最终中心。
非自愿记忆当然构成《追忆》中最具震动性的经验之一。但如果它成为唯一解释，小说中的误读、延宕、社交姿态、爱情迷误、音乐压力、视觉凝聚与艺术真理都会被压成“过去回来了”。

U1 does not reject memory. It uses memory as the first hinge through which Proustian reading moves from a single strong tradition toward a polycentric method.

Basic Literature Review as Method
The literature review in U1 should not be a bibliography dump. It should present reading positions: what each lens sees, what it risks, and how it returns to the Proustian text-world.









































Reading PositionWhat It SeesWhat It RisksReturn to TextMemory TraditionLost time returns through sensation, involuntary memory, and the sudden recovery of personal history.Reducing the novel to recollection, nostalgia, or psychological recovery.Ask what returns, and why the return is delayed, unstable, or transformed.DeleuzeSigns force thought; the narrator learns through error, apprenticeship, and interpretation.Flattening prose into taxonomy or turning Proust into Deleuze.Ask whether signs clarify the passage, or whether classification weakens its literary pressure.PouletMemory becomes space; moments and places condense into fields of vision.Freezing narrative movement into static contemplation.Ask what spatial image or mosaic-like arrangement the passage forms.Narrative DiscourseMeaning emerges through delay, order, duration, frequency, voice, retrospection, and narrative arrangement.Over-formalizing the text and losing the pressure of experience.Ask how the passage becomes readable only through narrative structure.Visual / Music / Sensory PathsProust transforms image, sound, smell, gesture, and atmosphere into literary form.Drifting into art history, musicology, or sensory history without textual return.Ask how the medium is absorbed by the novel rather than simply added to it.
Polycentric Reading｜No Center Does Not Mean No Judgment
U1 introduces a polycentric method. “No center” does not mean arbitrary wandering. It means no single theory is allowed to become sovereign. Each lens must become strong enough to make a claim, produce a problem, and submit itself to textual testing.
Rule 1｜No single theory owns Proust.
Memory, signs, space, narrative delay, music, visuality, and sensory history are all possible entrances, not final masters.
Rule 2｜Every lens must become strong.
A weak lens produces decoration. A strong lens produces a claim, a problem, and a pressure against other readings.
Rule 3｜The text tests every claim.
A theory is useful only when it returns to a sentence, scene, rhythm, object, gesture, sound, or misrecognition.
Claim / Problem Chain
This is the central writing method for U1. The goal is not to list themes, but to unfold claims until their problems, counterclaims, limits, and textual returns become visible.








































StepActionFunction1ClaimState what a reading position asserts.2PassageAttach the claim to a concrete Proust scene.3ProblemShow what the claim cannot easily explain.4Counter-ClaimLet another lens answer or resist it.5LimitExpose where the second lens also begins to fail.6ReturnGo back to the prose and form a judgment.

Method principle: The more fully a claim/problem chain is unfolded, the more testable, comparable, and recoverable the reading becomes. This is U1’s version of rigor.

Kite-Line Reading｜Textual Spine and Theoretical Lines
The hand-drawn model becomes the course’s visual method: theory flies outward from the text, reaches its horizon, dissolves, and returns.
English Formulation
The text is the spine.
Theories are lines released above it. Each line may fly outward, rise, diverge, and open a new field of vision. But every line must return to the Proustian text-world.
中文表述
文本是脊骨。
理论是在文本脊骨上方放飞的线束。每条理论线都可以飞出、分叉、升高，但最终必须重新降落到普鲁斯特的句子、场景、感官与叙事运动之中。

Proustian 2.0 does not reject theory. It releases theory from the text, lets it fly to its horizon, watches it dissolve, and then returns to the novel and to the reader’s own perception.

Reading Action｜U1 Trains Method, Not Sign Classification
The reading action no longer begins by asking “what kind of sign is this?” It begins with the passage and asks what pressure appears. Signs are one possible lens, not the center.

Start with a Proust passage, not a theory.
Identify the dominant pressure: memory, error, delay, image, sound, social gesture, sensation, or artistic form.
Choose one provisional lens: memory, signs, space, narrative discourse, visuality, music, or sensory history.
Ask what this lens makes visible in the passage.
Ask what this lens fails to see, weakens, or over-systematizes.
Let another lens answer, resist, or intensify the first claim.
Return to the prose: sentence, rhythm, scene, gesture, object, sound, or image.
Produce a readerly judgment: what did this passage teach the reader to see?

Core Lenses Opened by U1
U1 introduces several strong reading lenses. Each one is provisional. Each one must return to the passage.
Memory

What lost past returns?
What sensory shock triggers it?
Why is return not enough?

Signs

What pressure forces interpretation?
What does the narrator misread?
Where does apprenticeship begin?

Space / Vision

What spatial image forms?
How do moments and places become a mosaic?
What does vision compress?

Narrative Discourse

What is delayed?
Who knows what, and when?
How does narrative order make meaning possible?

Music / Visuality

How does another art enter the novel?
Does the novel imitate it or transform it?
What new form of truth appears?

Sensory / Social Space

How do smell, sound, room, salon, or street produce social time?
What historical pressure enters private experience?

Scene Anchors as Test Cases
These are not proof examples for a single theory. They are testing grounds where multiple lenses compete and return.
Madeleine
Memory, sensation, sign, habit, delay, and narrative reorganization.
Swann / Odette
Love, jealousy, deception, interpretation, social signs, and misreading.
Names of Places
Fantasy, expectation, disappointment, space, language, and desire.
Vinteuil
Music, love, ineffable truth, repetition, and artistic transformation.
Vermeer
Visual attention, art sign, mortality, color, detail, and judgment.
Transition to U2–U6
U1 opens the whole course. It does not close itself around Deleuze or signs. Its output is a method that can move into later units.








































Question Opened in U1Later UnitCourse FunctionWhy is memory powerful but insufficient?U2｜Memory / Time / SpaceTurns recollection into structure, delay, space, and passage-level reading.How do signs, errors, and forced thought train the reader?U1 bridge + U2Provides a portable method without making Deleuze the center.How does music become a path toward truth?U3｜Music / IneffableMoves from emotional motif to artistic and novelistic structure.How does seeing become attention and judgment?U4｜Visuality / GazeReads visual fragments as pressures on perception and form.How do spaces and sensations produce social time?U5｜Sensory History / Social SpaceLinks private sensation with historical and social form.How can reading become a reader-facing structure?U6｜Writing ApparatusConverts U1–U5 into pages, cards, labs, and course architecture.
Final Judgment
The center is not memory, not signs, not Deleuze, not Poulet, and not any single theory. The center is the disciplined effort to approach Proust’s novel through competing, testable, returnable reading paths.
